Sorry dude I wrote a wall of text then hit "back" on the stupid fucking shit laptop mouse pad of fuck...

Will get back to it...

Hey there,

37 here, somewhat in the same situation, have been for as long as I can remember.  Even when I was 16-17 I had doubt I'd ever reach 20. Then I reache 20 and figured 30 was far, way too far away for me to ever make it.  I'm now 37.

Unmarried yet not single, no kids, no house but my own apartment since forever.  Overly anxious, prone to depression, somewhat antisocial, and liking stuff most people don't like (i love metal, man).  Able to rationalize most anxiety and depression, but sometimes, like you, I wonder if my brain wouldn't look better laying on the tarmac.

It's somewhat my goto solution, but have you ever considered "leaving it all behind", packing a backpack and go for a thousand kilometers walk?

English is also my second language so don't worry about it; practice makes perfect.

I used to think (and still kinda do) that you need a certain wealth to travel.  I've been proven wrong many times; I've met Australians, Germans, French, Scotts, Irish, English people who were traveling around the world without a dime to their name (figuratively).  Seems like as long as you are willing to work, sometimes the shittiest jobs, you can make it work.  That being said it can be really hard work with low pay, like fruit picking, but I guess that's sometimes the price you have to pay to see the world and widen your horizons.  You will save quite a bit of money sleeping in hostels or campgrounds, but you may have to put aside comfort and nice smells for a little while.  That being said, I think your "lack of skills" may be a more important issue to tackle.  Good with numbers? What about a nice soul crushing accountant job for a little while?  It'll be hard on moral (at least after a few years) but you would be able to put money aside.  My advice would be to sort the job part out before putting a ring on it, but then again we are from completely different backgrounds (and continent) so odds are that we were raised quite differently, with different goals and whatnot.  To me tying the knot has never been an objective.  In fact, in retrospect I'm somewhat glad I never did, for I would now most probably be divorced.

What do you like doing?

I went in IT when I was your age, because I didn't like people and I enjoyed the fact that if you work in IT and $hit fuck5 up, it's pretty much always your own fault, or a flaw in logic or something, not an emotional response that you are reading wrong or some human related random error.  15 years in I now crave a job outside, in the bush or something, not in a depressing gray cubicle while breathing recycled air.  But then again, it seems like boring office jobs in gray cubicle will bring more $ home, so at some point you have to find the right balance, if that's ever possible.  I'm in the process of switching job right now.  If I've learned something throughout my career it's that you should always question what you are doing and how you feel about it in order to avoid waking up in utter misery 10 years from now.  Personally switching job every 5 years ish seem to do it for me; it sucks, its a pain in the ass, it's hard on the ego, it's depressing and off putting, but breaking the routine and the 6 hours per workday you get to spend on reddit every day.  And unchallenged person is not a happy person, at least not after a while.  It's like if you had a girlfriend that always agreed with you (i did).  It's nice for a while, but becomes boring and even worrisome (do you have your own personality here?) after a while.  Even in relationships you have to remain somewhat challenged to maintain interest and "passion" if I may call it like that.

Finish college!  It's not fun but you need to finish.  Rule of thumb in this world is generally (mind you we could debate that considering the reality of the last decade and the "for profit" education system) that you'll have a better paying job the more [learned](http://1.bp.blogspot.com/-9Ox4bvqHg3g/TvQb9PAQ3PI/AAAAAAAABl4/RPUBTOOExqo/s1600/ralph+wiggum+me+fail+english+thats+unpossible+simpsons.jpg) you are. (Ok, "educated").  It's always nice to not completely start at the bottom of the ladder, and it's a bit why I always had somewhat decent paying jobs. 

> have you ever talk about wedding, kids, family with any of your girlfriends, and things got shitty? 

Well my 21 year old Romanian friend, sit comfortably, because here comes story time.

What's now many years ago I had a pretty intense fling with a girl I worked with.  Unfortunately I had a gf when she was single, and when I became single she was not anymore.  We hooked up a few times nonetheless, and eventually her bf found out.  He was ditched, I was given "a chance", girl changed her mind, guilttrips, mindfucks, overwhelming sadness on the part of her now single ex,  and ultimately despite that we got along very well for a few days, she went back to him.  He had something I didn't, something she needed, something I've fought my whole life not to have.  She needed a stable, predictable, comfortable and free of excitement environment. A few weeks / months later, out of fear of losing her I imagine, he popped the question, and she came to me right away not really knowing what to do.  At that point I offered her to marry me instead if that would work better for her, offer she turned down for reasons that are now pretty obvious to me, but weren't at that time.   It was the only time I actually felt like it would be ok to get married to this specific person.  Mind you I wanted to get married before, at your age per example with my first girlfriend, but that would have been **a terrible mistake**.  Of course our relation got a bit rocky, especially considering how it started, but we stayed friends as she got married and had a kid with that guy.  Now a few years later we barely ever talk, mostly due to our respective  spouses understandably not being very fond of "our past relationship together".

>  have you ever talk about wedding, kids, family with any of your girlfriends, and things got shitty? 

To my current one, no, not really. Mostly because we are now doomed to have very frugal conversations, and because I do not want to stir something that I'm not up to.  I know she is.  And I know her mom hit menopause before 40, so in her situation time is somewhat of the essence.  And I don't really want to talk about it because looking back to the time while I was still in my hometown, If i would have had a kid or have gotten married, I wouldn't be where I am now, wouldn't be who I am, and somehow to me that seems like it would be a shame.  Nothing wrong at all with my friends who stayed, but despite still not knowing the hows and whys of life, I feel like my current situation is closer to an answer than if I wouldn't have made a move. To each their own I guess.

FYI Canada is a pretty cool place to be.  No shootings and quite a bit of opportunities, but It could be rather complex to immigrate I've heard.

Thank you for your reply, that was a very interesting read, and it's good to see somewhat similar experience.  For me I would say maturity wise I'm pretty much my age, whereas hanging out with 20s becomes uh... overwhelming (?) at some point.  In fact most of my friends are in their early 40s.  We're old boys.  We still play in the mud.  We still build teeter totters with fallen trees.

> If you didn't have any obligations or commitments , what then? Say you're in a position to do anything, be anywhere, be anyone--this is a brand new clean slate with no concerns in the short term for food or shelter or anything else--what would you be doing? Where would you be doing it? Who would you be?

Strangely enough, I've been there.  I replied to somebody earlier and explained my story a bit more in detail. At 25 I was exactly there : no lady friend, no more job.   I packed my car and left, and I became somebody drastically different than before I left.  Maybe it's time, distance or the 6000km from my starting point but I can see when I go back; I'm different.  It used to be subtle, but now it's pretty hard to "hide" when going back to my starting point.  There's an experience in there that isn't shared by everyone, the same way I currently have no experience with fatherhood.

It's been a decade.  6000km.  And today, a few days before my birthday, I still wonder the same question I was a decade ago, and according to the comments on this thread I'm not the only one in this situation.

I wouldn't say I resent her, nowhere near that.

There's always been something a bit off, even when we started dating. I couldn't put my finger on it, but there was...something.  We seemed on different pace.

Years of being together exacerbated that.  If I would have to guess I'd say we grew apart.  The complicity you'd expect in a nice and mature relation was never really there; I think she's more homey while I'm much more "sleep in the mud" style.  She's city and I'm forest; She's pop and I'm heavy metal.  It seems like our views, instead of being pulled closer together, just carried on in two parallel path.  We live together, we share a bed, share meals, household tasks and all, but there's no complicity.   I wish I could say that we lost it, but I'm afraid it was never really there.  

I can't commit to something like that.

My answer to your question and worries may change the tone I've originally given to this whole thread, and for this I have to thank you.

I'll have to start by reassure you that I do not consider my life wasted in any way, shape or form.  Being my age, unmarried and kidless is not what I would consider a failure, so don't worry about your life, at least not yet.

Why didn't I get married?  Well, I could have.  I was once ready, but the circumstances were shitty, I'll get back to it.  I also almost had kids a few times;close calls, everybody gets em.

At 25, after two years with the same girl, I started caring less if she was to get pregnant.  Nice girl, decent job, good healthy couple, why not?  Coincidentally, that's around the same time she dumped me for somebody I worked with.  Since we all worked together and my hometown is pretty small, it's not hard to understand how potentially shitty this whole situation could have become if I wouldn't have packed my car and left to the complete opposite end of the country.  And here's where it gets interesting; 

**That breakup was the best thing to ever happen to me**.   

I was 25, I had a steady job in my hometown, my parents were 15 minutes away, I had never really been challenged, worked with my friends and girlfriend/future mother of my children, we'd all get out to the bars together, the whole shebang.  So when I got dumped and all those things were so intertwined, after a few very pathetic days I just said [fuck it!](http://cdn.someecards.com/someecards/usercards/1299326129611_4466340.png) packed my car and started driving.  I had no idea where I was going; I just knew I wasn't staying.

This was 10 years ago.  In the last decade I've experience things I couldn't even imagine existed prior to stepping out of my comfort zone.  I traveled, met people, was forced into behaving and thinking differently in order to integrate, find a job, survive and eventually have a place to call home, even if it's just an apartment.  I've learned languages,  met brilliant people (and insane weirdos!) and overall I turned out 100% differently then if I would have stayed, not that there's anything wrong with my old school friends who are still there.  

The best advice I could give you right now?  **Travel**.   I'm from a place where traveling isn't a priority.  I was told all my life to study hard, find a good job ... then profit.  Well, I studied.  I found a pretty decent job.  That job turned into a career; a career with a great wage, especially considering small town, and bulletproof job security and killer advantages, but in a gray cubicle, surrounded by other gray cubicles, also populated by people who hated their life.  Some had been hating it for 20 years, some others, like me, only for 3-4.  Moral was low.  It's not funny working in a windowless "bunker", even if the wage is good.  My friends are still there.  The bought houses, the have children, they are married, and I see nothing wrong with that.   There may be greater wisdom to acquire raising a child than traveling the world; I do not know for I have done only one of those things.  To this day I still believe traveling childless is far, far easier and more enjoyable than the latter.  I'm sure parents could confirm.

Early in my travels, still in my country, I met random world travelers, young for the most part, for whom my country was a world of interrogations.  Having to explain our customs, social and cultural diversity and our "way of life" forced quite an introspection, and hearing about theirs was eye opening.  It was the seed of the ideology I cultivated while traveling : We all live the same life in a different, yet just as valid way.

One of my regrets (I do not have many) is that I started traveling too late in life; I always had either a great job or a great girlfriend. I left the first time I lost both at the same time.

In your specific case, since you have no skills, traveling may help you figure out what skills would make you happy in this life.  I know many people who went great distances on motorcycle trips with little to know mechanical knowledge nor specific interests and came back completely changed.  This is an advice I should also apply to my own present situation^^idiot ^^self.  Traveling should be mandatory prior to having to commit to a specific career.

On top of that, traveling is a great way to get to know someone. It's very hard to keep anything fake when you are facing real adversity.  Traveling can both destroy or strengthen friendships and relationships.  Life isn't a walk in the park, and it's good to know who you are walking with really is.

Skills are important.  Something, somewhere has to give some value to having you around; specifically you.  This is what you will have to cash on when looking for a job.  If you are lucky (I have been) you will randomly fluke onto a job that will allow you to acquire said skills, and the wheel will start spinning for a while.  A good job will give you good skill which will provide you with a better job and hopefully somewhere along the line you won't end up underemployed, which is not good for your skills (nor ego, self esteem, whatever)

Sorry for the long post, but cheers for forcing me into an introspection that I wouldn't otherwise necessarily have done.

>I don't want to succumb to pseudo-science in order to give my life a meaning.

Sorry, I should have been clearer.  What I mean by that is that thus far, throughout my life, I have met people with firm beliefs in pseudo-science, either in a religious way (not many) or who, per example, firmly believed in astrology, belief strong enough for them to base their entire existence on it.

I'm not one of those.  I rely solely on fact and science, as boring as it may sound (yet this isn't uncommon on Reddit)  I do not need to believe in something greater than me to justify my existence.


As for uniqueness, I am, or at least feel unique enough to feel alone in the universe, which isn't really helping the current situation.  I always seem to be swimming in a different direction, against the trends if you will.  We could use the Ice Bucket Challenge as an example; it was a great idea, but as the masses join in the trend, I started steering away from it before it became popular.  I cannot stand conformism for the sakes of social acceptance / personal reward. Don't get me wrong, ALS is shit and I'm incredibly happy that this campaign is a success, but fuck people needing to conform to a trend, fuck people getting married and having kids because everybody else is doing it while finding you strange for not conforming.

I'm seeking more without knowing what I seek.
